facts.text: Grad B said that setting up all the probabilities for a flat, single-layer structure (all features pointing directly to one output node) would be a pain.
facts.source_quote: Reasons being , you know , it 'd be a pain to set up all the probabilities for that .

facts.text: Grad B said that if they later added a learning step on top of the flat structure, not knowing belief-nets well would leave the team handicapped.
facts.source_quote: If we moved onto the next step and did learning of some sort , uh according Bhaskara we 'd be handicapped . I don't know belief - nets very well .

facts.text: Grad C explained that with N features feeding directly into a single node, the number of probability values needed grows exponentially with N (two to the N).
facts.source_quote: If you have N features , then it 's two to the N {disfmarker} {pause} or exponential in N .

facts.text: Grad B said the flat structure also 'wouldn't look pretty,' with Grad C adding that it would mean all the features pointing to a single node.
facts.source_quote: And they wouldn't look pretty . So .

facts.text: Grad B said their next idea, instead of the flat one-layer structure, was to add a middle layer to the belief net.
facts.source_quote: So then our next idea was to add a middle layer , right ?

facts.text: Grad B explained that the features drawn from the user's communication represent an abstract idea the person is trying to convey — for example, being a tourist who wants to go to a particular place.
facts.source_quote: the person at the screen is trying to communicate some abstract idea , like " I 'm {disfmarker} " the {disfmarker} the abstract idea being " I am a tourist I want to go {pause} to this place . "

facts.text: Grad B said the middle layer was meant to capture a hidden concept — such as whether the user is a tourist or running an errand — that could not be directly extracted from the data.
facts.source_quote: the middle thing , we were thinking along the lines of maybe trying to figure out , like , the concept of whether they 're a tourist {pause} or {pause} whether they 're running an errand or something like that along those lines

facts.text: Grad B listed the hidden variables devised for the middle layer: whether the person was on a tour, running an errand, or in a hurry.
facts.source_quote: the hidden variables {disfmarker} hair variables we came up with were whether someone was on a tour , running an errand , or whether they were in a hurry

facts.text: The reasoning behind the 'hurry' variable was that someone in a hurry would be less likely to want to view things ('do Vista'), since, as Grad C put it, wanting to view things is inconsistent with being in a hurry.
facts.source_quote: Because {pause} if you want to view things you wouldn't be in a hurry .

facts.text: Grad B suggested that a hurried person might instead be using their stated destination merely as a navigational waypoint toward another place, rather than as the actual goal.
facts.source_quote: they might be more likely to be using the place that they want to go to as a {disfmarker} like a {pause} navigational point to go to another place .

facts.text: Grad B mentioned two more candidate middle-layer variables: whether the destination was the person's final destination, and whether the destination was closed.
facts.source_quote: Whether the destination was their final destination , whether the destination was closed .

facts.text: Grad B noted that the belief-net was still a rough 'toy' implementation at that point, because the team did not yet know the necessary probabilities.
